messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 53
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Bus Driver
- Trauma Type: Rape
- Pcl5: 76

**Patient Vignette: Mark**

Mark is a 53-year-old married man who has worked as a city bus driver for over twenty years. He presents for therapy at the urging of his wife, who has grown increasingly concerned about his withdrawal, irritability, and what she calls his “ghost-like” presence at home. He has been on medical leave from work for the past six weeks.

The event that shattered Mark’s world happened eight months ago, in late November. He had finished his last run of the night, a quiet shift through the industrial edge of the city. A passenger, a young man who had been riding for several stops without incident, lingered near the back door as Mark pulled into the depot. Mark asked him to exit, and the man complied, but as Mark stepped off the bus to lock up, the man reappeared from the shadows. He forced Mark back onto the bus, into the driver’s cabin, and raped him at knifepoint. Mark remembers the cold blade against his throat, the smell of diesel and sweat, and the hum of the engine he had left idling. He remembers thinking, *If I just stay very still, it will end faster.*

Afterward, the man simply walked away. Mark sat in the driver’s seat for an hour, unable to move. He did not call the police. He drove home, showered, and told his wife he had been held up. He said he was fine. He believed that if he didn’t say the word *rape*, it hadn’t truly happened.

But his body knew. Within weeks, Mark could no longer drive his route. The moment a passenger stood too close to his seat, or when a young man boarded alone at night, his heart would pound so hard he felt dizzy. He began to avoid the night shift entirely, swapping with younger drivers who didn’t ask questions. He started checking his mirrors obsessively, not for traffic, but for faces. Every male passenger under thirty became a potential threat. He began taking longer, circuitous routes to avoid the depot where it happened. His supervisor noted his erratic driving and told him to take time off.

At home, Mark is a different man. He no longer sleeps in the same bed as his wife. He spends nights on the couch, fully dressed, with the lights on and the television playing infomercials. He says it’s because he has “bad dreams,” but he does not describe them. In truth, he wakes several times a night, drenched in sweat, his hand reaching for a knife he no longer carries. He avoids sex entirely. When his wife touches his shoulder, he flinches. He has not been able to explain why. He feels a profound, corrosive shame, as though he has been permanently dirtied.

The world feels dangerous now. He cannot go to the grocery store without scanning every aisle. He stopped attending his son’s hockey games because the crowd felt too close. He has become hypervigilant in a way that exhausts him. He drinks three to four beers every evening to quiet his mind, but it only makes the intrusive images—the knife, the engine hum, the man’s breath—more vivid before sleep.

Mark does not see himself as a victim. He says, “I should have fought back. I’m a grown man. I drove a bus for twenty years. I should have done something.” He feels emasculated, hollow. His wife has begged him to talk to her, but he cannot find the words. He is terrified that if he says it out loud, the shame will drown him. He came to therapy only after she threatened to leave, and he sits in the chair with his arms crossed, looking out the window, as if waiting for the session to end before it begins.
